domain_reasoning: Most of the work is reviewing, merging, and updating records in the defect-tracking system.
length_reasoning: A small, well-maintained list can be reviewed in an hour, while a release with many stale or duplicate records can require a full working day or more.
review_reasoning: The QA lead checks the current list and samples changed records, with more cross-checking for a typical pass.
stakes_reasoning: An incorrect status or workaround can mislead users or testers, while an omitted serious known issue can contribute to a damaging release.
context_reasoning: Recognizing duplicates and accurate workarounds requires familiarity with the product and its defect history.

domain_reasoning: Verification usually involves operating the application and test environment, then updating the defect ticket.
length_reasoning: A straightforward fix can be retested in minutes, while a complex defect may require substantial setup and regression checks.
review_reasoning: A colleague checks the ticket and evidence for a simple fix, and examines test results and relevant conditions for a typical one.
stakes_reasoning: An incorrectly closed defect can reach users and require rework, while a serious missed defect can cause an outage or data loss.
context_reasoning: Verification depends on the product's behavior, test environments, and defect workflow.

domain_reasoning: The specialist gathers device and warranty details and opens and updates cases in vendor and internal systems.
length_reasoning: A referral with available warranty details is quick, while gathering diagnostics and navigating a vendor's requirements takes longer.
review_reasoning: A reviewer checks the referral against the ticket and warranty information, with more detail to inspect in a typical case.
stakes_reasoning: An incomplete referral typically delays service and can be corrected, although a consequential delay may prolong an outage.
context_reasoning: The specialist needs the employer's escalation procedures, inventory records, and vendor arrangements.

domain_reasoning: Apart from talking, the specialist mainly uses support tools, documentation, and the affected application or device.
length_reasoning: Simple how-to questions take a few minutes, while troubleshooting and confirming a fix can take substantially longer.
review_reasoning: A reviewer listens to or reads the contact and checks any associated support record.
stakes_reasoning: Incorrect advice usually causes a repeat contact or reversible disruption, but advice affecting settings or files can cause data loss.
context_reasoning: Effective support requires familiarity with the organization's applications, access procedures, and common issues.

domain_reasoning: Most of the work is composing a clear written response from an inquiry or an already established investigation result.
length_reasoning: A standard answer can be sent quickly, while a complex claim result requires a more carefully tailored explanation.
review_reasoning: A reviewer compares the message with the account context and checks that the result or adjustment is accurately stated.
stakes_reasoning: An inaccurate response usually prompts a complaint or correction, but a material misstatement about a claim can create financial or regulatory exposure.
context_reasoning: The representative needs the organization's correspondence standards, product terms, and account procedures.

domain_reasoning: The representative uses the case system to gather details, select the receiving department, and submit the referral.
length_reasoning: A well-documented grievance can be routed quickly, while a complicated history takes longer to summarize and classify.
review_reasoning: The reviewer checks the receiving department and compares the referral summary with the underlying case.
stakes_reasoning: A poor referral usually delays resolution and creates rework, but misrouting a time-sensitive regulated complaint can create regulatory exposure.
context_reasoning: Correct routing requires knowledge of the organization's departments, escalation rules, and case system.

domain_reasoning: The specialist spends most of the assessment using the product, reviewing specifications, and comparing options in applications or websites.
length_reasoning: A familiar upgrade can be assessed in a few hours, while a broader product evaluation requires testing, comparison, and a written recommendation.
review_reasoning: A manager checks the recommendation and supporting comparisons, with more scrutiny of evidence and assumptions for a typical evaluation.
stakes_reasoning: A faulty recommendation can lead to an unsuitable purchase, wasted spending, or disruption when an upgrade is adopted.
context_reasoning: The evaluation needs familiarity with the organization's existing equipment, user requirements, and support constraints.

domain_reasoning: Apart from talking, the representative mainly consults the customer account and records the contact in the service system.
length_reasoning: A simple result can be explained in a few minutes, while a disputed claim or several follow-up questions make the call longer.
review_reasoning: A reviewer listens to the recorded call and checks the result against the account record.
stakes_reasoning: An incorrect explanation can cause a complaint or require a correction, while a material claim misstatement can create financial or regulatory exposure.
context_reasoning: The representative needs the employer's account tools, claim procedures, and communication rules.

domain_reasoning: The analyst investigates software behavior by examining logs, configuration, and code and may run diagnostic tests.
length_reasoning: An obvious error or known configuration issue may be identified quickly, while tracing an unfamiliar failure can take several hours.
review_reasoning: A developer checks the cited evidence and likely source, with more log or code tracing for a typical diagnosis.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong initial diagnosis usually leads to developer rework, but it can delay resolution of a serious production issue.
context_reasoning: Tracing a failure efficiently often requires deep familiarity with the system's architecture and failure history.

domain_reasoning: The coordinator uses scheduling, communication, access-management, and test-management tools to arrange and brief the participants.
length_reasoning: A small round using existing scripts can be organized in a few hours, while coordinating multiple participants and access needs can take several working days of active effort.
review_reasoning: The QA manager checks coverage, participant instructions, scheduling, and access, sampling more materials for a typical round.
stakes_reasoning: A scheduling or briefing mistake usually delays testing or leaves gaps that can be corrected, while improper access can expose sensitive data.
context_reasoning: Organizing the round requires familiarity with the product, stakeholders, test environments, and access processes.

domain_reasoning: Apart from the conversation, the analyst mainly inspects application behavior, logs, and diagnostic tools during the session.
length_reasoning: A familiar issue may be diagnosed in a short session, while an intermittent or difficult issue requires a longer joint investigation.
review_reasoning: A reviewer checks a recording and any diagnostic evidence and agreed next steps, with a longer session taking more time.
stakes_reasoning: A mistaken diagnosis usually causes further investigation or customer inconvenience, but a missed serious fault can prolong an outage or data-loss risk.
context_reasoning: Diagnosis depends on the product's architecture, known issues, and the customer's environment.

domain_reasoning: The analyst primarily reads requirements and writes the scope, approach, coverage, and risks in a test plan.
length_reasoning: A small change can use a concise plan, while a major release requires substantially more analysis of scope, dependencies, and risks.
review_reasoning: The lead compares the plan with requirements and risks, examining more coverage and dependencies for a typical plan.
stakes_reasoning: A coverage gap can allow defects to reach users, and a missed critical scenario can contribute to an outage or data loss.
context_reasoning: A useful plan requires knowledge of the product, release process, environments, and business risks.

domain_reasoning: The study involves gathering workflow and cost information, comparing alternatives in applications, and preparing a report.
length_reasoning: A limited study with accessible data can take a working day, while a multi-department study with layout and cost comparisons can take several days of active work.
review_reasoning: Management reviews the recommendation and checks key assumptions, calculations, and supporting workflow evidence.
stakes_reasoning: An incorrect feasibility recommendation can lead to a costly investment or disruptive workflow and space changes.
context_reasoning: The study requires knowledge of local workflows, facilities, costs, and organizational constraints.

domain_reasoning: Apart from talking, the representative mainly examines account, usage, billing, and relevant reference information in service systems.
length_reasoning: An obvious usage or billing explanation can be checked quickly, while a complaint spanning several periods or possible causes takes longer.
review_reasoning: A reviewer checks the recorded contact and compares the explanation with the account and usage information.
stakes_reasoning: A mistaken explanation can cause a repeat complaint or delayed correction, while mishandling a significant billing dispute can create financial or regulatory exposure.
context_reasoning: The representative needs the utility or employer's account tools, billing rules, and complaint procedures.

domain_reasoning: Feature-level cases are typically written as test steps, inputs, and expected results rather than implemented as automated code.
length_reasoning: A simple feature needs only a few cases, while complex rules and edge conditions require a much larger set.
review_reasoning: The reviewer compares cases with requirements and checks expected outcomes, sampling more scenarios in a typical set.
stakes_reasoning: Missing or incorrect cases can leave defects undetected, with critical gaps potentially allowing serious failures into production.
context_reasoning: Designing effective cases requires familiarity with the feature's business rules, product behavior, and test conventions.

domain_reasoning: The representative selects disposition codes and enters the summary and actions in the customer-record system.
length_reasoning: A routine contact takes less than a minute to record, while a complicated interaction needs a fuller summary and several entries.
review_reasoning: A reviewer compares the saved record with the contact, spending longer on a typical interaction than on a brief one.
stakes_reasoning: A poor record usually causes rework or confusion for the next agent, although missing documentation of a regulated complaint can create exposure.
context_reasoning: Accurate coding and notes require familiarity with the employer's CRM, dispositions, and recordkeeping standards.

domain_reasoning: The analyst mainly organizes observations from an already evaluated build into written feedback and recommendations.
length_reasoning: A short note about a single issue can be written quickly, while consolidating several usability and functionality findings takes longer.
review_reasoning: A developer or product owner checks the note against the build and supporting observations, with more findings to verify in a typical note.
stakes_reasoning: Unclear or incorrect feedback generally leads to rework or a usability problem that can be corrected in a later build.
context_reasoning: Useful recommendations depend on the product's intended users, workflows, and design conventions.
